analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to warn, bargain with, and train workers whose jobs automation threatens.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 116th Congress ended, having drawn a single sponsor and zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies with 25 or more employees to give workers 180 to 270 days' written notice before technology changes or eliminates their jobs, and to bargain with the workers (or an elected employee committee) about how the technology could fit their skills. Employers would have to provide paid, on-the-clock training, and workers who lose their jobs would get at least a year of training, first crack at new openings, six months of severance, and an $8,000 voucher for training toward a new occupation. Retaliation against workers who assert these rights would be prohibited, with lawsuits and daily fines backing it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies with 25 or more employees whose jobs would be changed or eliminated by automation, artificial intelligence, or other computerized systems. They would get months of advance warning, paid training during work hours without any cut in pay, and — if their job disappears outright — a year of training, priority hiring for open positions, six months of severance pay, and an $8,000 voucher for retraining in a new occupation, all shielded from federal income tax. Labor unions and elected employee committees would gain a seat at the table before new technology is installed, and workers could enforce the law in court with back pay, punitive damages, and attorney's fees.

how_it_helps.text: Employers would have to bargain with workers' representatives 180 days before deploying technology that changes or eliminates jobs, and give affected employees written notice describing the technology and its impact on positions.

Workers whose positions change would get on-the-job training during work hours with no reduction in pay or benefits, supplemented where needed by employer-paid apprenticeship or college-credential training.

Workers who lose their jobs to technology would get at least one year of employer-provided training, priority hiring for new or open positions for a year, six months of severance pay on the day of the loss, and an $8,000 voucher for training toward a new occupation.
Workers who also lack basic credentials such as a high school diploma would receive an additional 180 days of basic-skills training, on top of any other training owed.

The law would be enforceable: workers or their representatives could sue for back pay, lost benefits, punitive damages, and reinstatement, with attorney's fees awarded, and the Labor Department or state attorneys general could act on workers' behalf; employers could also face fines of up to $5,000 per employee per day.
Severance, the retraining voucher, and court-awarded back pay would be excluded from taxable income, so workers would keep the full amounts.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — any business enterprise engaged in interstate commerce with at least 25 employees, including part-timers. They would bear the cost of advance notice, mandatory bargaining, paid training (indefinite in length for position changes, at least a year for job losses), six months of severance, $8,000 vouchers, and potential fines of up to $5,000 per employee per day, plus litigation costs. Franchised, parent, and integrated companies could be jointly on the hook, and contractors who fail the bill's independent-contractor test would count as employees.

drawbacks.text: The mandates are expensive and open-ended: employers would owe up to 270 days' notice, training with 'no regard to the length of time' it takes, a year of training plus six months of severance for displaced workers, and fines of up to $5,000 per employee per day for violations — a heavy burden for firms just above the 25-employee threshold.

Requiring bargaining and mediation 180 days before any job-affecting technology could delay automation, e-commerce, and other computerized systems, and raise the risk that companies outsource or relocate work instead of adopting the technology domestically.
The private right of action allows punitive and consequential damages plus mandatory attorney's fees, which would expose employers to litigation costs well beyond actual harm.

The bill bars the Labor Department from issuing regulations (beyond defining 'technology'), leaving employers to rely on nonbinding guidance for compliance, which could create uncertainty about what counts as good faith.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers facing displacement by automation, the protections are substantial and unusually concrete: advance notice, paid retraining, severance, hiring priority, and real enforcement tools, with the benefits tax-free. The costs fall entirely on mid-size and large employers, and an honest supporter would concede that the combination of mandatory pre-deployment bargaining, unlimited-duration training, and six months of severance is among the most demanding technology-transition mandates ever proposed federally, which helps explain why not a single colleague — from either party — signed on. The bill's one-sided enforcement design (punitive damages plus daily fines plus fees) also invites litigation that small compliance mistakes could trigger.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the Workers' Right to Training Act on September 11, 2019.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no hearing, markup, or floor action ever followed.
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with 25 or more employees, who avoided entirely the bill's notice, bargaining, paid-training, severance, and fine requirements; no worker received any benefit because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, who avoided new training and severance costs

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case that workers displaced by technology deserve notice, training, and severance; recruited no cosponsors before the bill stalled.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — allowing it to die when the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so a partisan split never formed on the record.

industries.industry: Mid-size and large employers adopting automation (retail, manufacturing, logistics, finance)
industries.note: Firms with 25+ employees would bear the full cost of advance notice, mandatory bargaining, paid retraining, six months of severance, and per-day fines whenever they deploy job-changing technology. The bill's cost to them is precisely the protection it delivers to workers.

industries.industry: Gig platforms and staffing firms reliant on contractors
industries.note: The bill defines 'employee' using the strict independent-contractor test and treats franchisors and integrated or parent companies as joint employers, which would pull many contractor-based and fissured workplaces into its notice, training, and severance obligations.

industries.industry: Community colleges, apprenticeship programs, and workforce training providers
industries.note: Employers would have to pay for apprenticeship programs and credential-bearing courses, and displaced workers choosing training for a new occupation would receive $8,000 vouchers usable at any eligible training provider — a new, guaranteed funding stream for these institutions.

Union representatives would automatically conduct the mandated pre-technology bargaining for represented workers, giving organized labor a formal say over automation decisions at every covered workplace; nonunion workers would elect their own committees.
